The infrared spectrum of a compound is shown below.

![IR spectrum showing a strong absorption at approximately 1720 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](assets/001-ir-spectrum-showing-a-strong-absorption-at-appro.png)

Which compound is shown by the infrared spectrum?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Butanal contains a C=O (carbonyl) group, which gives the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**A** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 1500–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to C=C, therefore the compound cannot be but-1-ene.

**B** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (alcohol), therefore the compound cannot be butan-1-ol.

**D** is incorrect as there is no absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to O-H (acid), therefore the compound cannot be butanoic acid.

parts.problem_md: Which of the following statements about propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO, and propanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, is **not** correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The molecular ion peak (M<sup>+</sup>) is the peak with the highest *m/e* ratio, excluding any peaks due to heavier isotopes.
- Both propanal and propanone have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O and so both have a molecular ion peak at *m/e* = 58.

  - Propanal arises from the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO<sup>+</sup> ion.
  - Propanone arises from the CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> ion.
- Propanal mass spectrum

![Mass spectrum of propanal (CH3CH2CHO) showing molecular ion peak at m/e = 58 and characteristic fragmentation pattern](assets/002-mass-spectrum-of-propanal-ch3ch2cho-showing-mole.jpg)

- Propanone mass spectrum

![Mass spectrum of propanone (CH3COCH3) showing molecular ion peak at m/e = 58 and characteristic fragmentation pattern](assets/003-mass-spectrum-of-propanone-ch3coch3-showing-mole.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as propanal and propanone do have a different fingerprint region in the infrared spectrum.

**B** is incorrect as both compounds show absorption in the infrared spectrum due to the C=O bond.

**C** is incorrect as propanal and propanone do have different fragmentation patterns in the mass spectrum.

parts.problem_md:
The infrared spectrum below shows an unknown compound.

![IR spectrum showing C-H absorptions at 2700 to 2950 cm-1 including a characteristic aldehyde C-H doublet, and a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1720 cm-1 with no O-H absorption](assets/004-ir-spectrum-showing-c-h-absorptions-at-2700-to-2.jpg)

Which compound would give this spectrum?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The spectrum shows a strong absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of a C=O (carbonyl) bond in an aldehyde.
- C-H absorptions are visible at 2850–2950 cm<sup>-1</sup> (alkyl C-H) and at approximately 2700–2820 cm<sup>-1</sup> (the characteristic aldehyde C-H doublet).
- Butanal is an aldehyde and contains a C=O group consistent with the spectrum.

![Skeletal formula of butanal](assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-butanal.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 1-bromobutane contains no C=O bond and would show no absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

![Skeletal formula of 1-bromobutane](assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-1-bromobutane.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as butan-1-ol would show a strong O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the hydroxyl group, with no C=O absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

![Skeletal formula of butan-1-ol](assets/007-skeletal-formula-of-butan-1-ol.jpg)

**D** is incorrect as butanoic acid would show a broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the carboxyl group, in addition to the C=O absorption.

![Skeletal formula of butanoic acid](assets/008-skeletal-formula-of-butanoic-acid.jpg)

parts.problem_md:
The infrared spectrum below shows an unknown compound.

![IR spectrum showing a sharp O-H absorption at 3200 to 3600 cm-1 and a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1700 to 1740 cm-1, with complex fingerprint region absorptions](assets/009-ir-spectrum-showing-a-sharp-o-h-absorption-at-32.jpg)

Which compound could have produced the infrared spectrum?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The spectrum shows an absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of the O-H bond in an alcohol.
- The spectrum also shows an absorption at approximately 1700–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>, characteristic of a C=O (carbonyl) bond in a ketone or aldehyde.
- The compound contains both an alcohol O-H and a ketone C=O; the O-H of a carboxylic acid absorbs at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which is not observed here.

**A** is incorrect as butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid whose O-H absorption appears at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, not at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> as shown in the spectrum.

**C** is incorrect as pent-4-en-1-ol contains a C=C bond that would produce a characteristic absorption at 1500–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup>, which is absent in this spectrum.

**D** is incorrect as pent-4-en-2-one does not contain an O-H bond, but the spectrum shows an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Note the position of the O-H absorption carefully:
> 
> - In alcohols it appears at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> - In carboxylic acids it is a broader absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> A common error is to label the C-H absorption (2850–2950 cm<sup>-1</sup>) as O-H.

parts.problem_md: Which of the following **cannot** be obtained from an infrared spectrum?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Infrared spectroscopy measures the absorption of infrared radiation by molecules, which is used to identify functional groups based on the bond strength and mass of the atoms involved.
- It is not used to determine the molecular mass.

  - A mass spectrometer is used for this.

**A** is incorrect as the identity of a compound can be determined by comparing its infrared spectrum with reference spectra.

**C** is incorrect as the presence of C=O bonds can be detected from the infrared spectrum.

**D** is incorrect as the presence of O-H bonds can be detected from the infrared spectrum.

parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A carboxylic acid shows two key absorptions in the infrared spectrum:
- The C=O bond absorbs at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
- The O-H bond in carboxylic acids produces a broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**A** is incorrect as an alcohol would only show an O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup> characteristic of a carboxylic acid.

**B** is incorrect as an aldehyde would only show a C=O absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as a ketone would only show a C=O absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> and not the broad O-H absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problem_md: Which class of compound does **not** contain the functional group responsible for the strong absorption between 1670 cm<sup>-1</sup> and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> is characteristic of the C=O (carbonyl) bond, found in aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids.
- Alcohols do not contain a C=O bond; the characteristic absorption of an alcohol is the O-H bond at 3200–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as aldehydes contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**C** is incorrect as carboxylic acids contain a C=O bond as part of the carboxyl group, which absorbs between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**D** is incorrect as ketones contain a C=O bond, which produces the characteristic absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three key infrared absorptions to learn for CIE IAL Chemistry are:
> 
> - O-H (alcohol): 3230–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - C=O (aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid): 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> - O-H (carboxylic acid, broad): 2500–3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problem_md: Which of the following infrared spectra could show a carboxylic acid?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- A carboxylic acid shows a broad O-H absorption from 2500 to 3000 cm<sup>-1</sup>, caused by hydrogen bonding of the carboxyl O-H group, in addition to a strong C=O absorption at approximately 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of an alcohol, identified by the sharp O-H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no C=O absorption present.

**C** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of an ester, showing a strong C=O absorption between 1710 and 1750 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no O-H absorption.

**D** is incorrect as this is the IR spectrum of a ketone, identified by the strong C=O absorption at approximately 1710 cm<sup>-1</sup> with no O-H absorption.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Ethanol at 3400 cm<sup>-1</sup>: O−H bond **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanal at 1720 cm<sup>-1</sup>: C=O bond **[1 mark]**

The isomers **A** and **B**, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, both form an orange precipitate when reacted with 2,4-DNPH.

**A** is unbranched and reacts with alkaline I<sub>2</sub> (aq) to produce a yellow precipitate.

**B** does not react with alkaline I<sub>2</sub> (aq). It contains a chiral centre and produces a silver mirror when warmed with Tollens' reagent.

Draw the structure of the yellow precipitate produced by the reaction between **A** and alkaline I<sub>2</sub> (aq).
parts.solution_md:
The structure of the yellow precipitate is:

![Displayed formula of triiodomethane (CHI3), the yellow precipitate from the iodoform reaction](assets/020-displayed-formula-of-triiodomethane-chi3-the-yel.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of triiodomethane (CHI<sub>3</sub>): carbon bonded to one hydrogen and three iodine atoms

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> The reaction occurs when a methyl ketone (or ethanol) is warmed with alkaline I<sub>2</sub> (aq). Compound **A** has a straight chain and gives a positive iodoform test, confirming it is a methyl ketone: pentan-2-one (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).

There are three possible isomers, **A**, **B** and **C**, with the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.

Isomers **A** and **B** are positional isomers of each other.

Isomer **C** is a functional group isomer of **A** and **B**.

The percentage by mass of carbon in all three isomers is 60.0%.

Calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in all three isomers.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage by mass of hydrogen and oxygen in C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (3 x 12.0) + (8 x 1.0) + 16.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass of each element:

% by mass = $\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{element}}{\mathrm{overall} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{compound}}$ x 100

% by mass of H = $\frac{8.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 13.3%

% by mass of O = $\frac{16.0}{60.0}$ x 100 = 26.7%

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 60.0
> 
> 1 mark for % H = 13.3% **AND** % O = 26.7%
> 
> Percentages given to 2 significant figures are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> All three isomers have the same molecular formula, so they all have the same percentage by mass for each element.
> 
> To find percentage by mass: divide the total mass of the element in one molecule by *M*<sub>r</sub>, then multiply by 100.
> 
> Check your answer:
> 
> 60.0 + 13.3 + 26.7 = 100.0

Explain why infrared spectroscopy alone could not be used to distinguish between compounds **X** and **Y**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Infrared spectroscopy could not be used to distinguish between **X** and **Y** because:
> 
> - They both contain the same key functional group
> **OR**
> They both contain a C=O bond and no other distinguishing functional group
> **OR**
> They are both carbonyl compounds **[1 mark]**
> - Both spectra would show an absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup> due to the C=O bond, with no other key distinguishing absorption **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **X** is a ketone (butan-2-one) and compound **Y** is an aldehyde (2-methylpropanal). Both functional groups contain a C=O bond that absorbs at 1670–1740 cm<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups by their characteristic absorptions. When two compounds share the same functional group and have no other distinguishing groups, their IR spectra look the same in the key regions above 1500 cm<sup>-1</sup>. This is why IR alone cannot distinguish between them.
> 
> To distinguish between an aldehyde and a ketone, chemical tests (such as Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution) or mass spectrometry would be needed.

> 
> - *m*/*e* = 28 **[1 mark]**
> - Formula: CO<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **Y** is an aldehyde (2-methylpropanal). Aldehydes produce a characteristic CHO<sup>+</sup> fragment at *m*/*e* = 29. This can lose a hydrogen atom to give CO<sup>+</sup> at *m*/*e* = 28.

> Compound **X** is a ketone (butan-2-one). Ketones undergo α-cleavage to give acylium ions such as CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> (*m*/*e* = 43), but do not readily produce CO<sup>+</sup> at *m*/*e* = 28.
> 
> This difference in fragmentation patterns allows mass spectrometry to distinguish between the two isomers even though they have the same *M*<sub>r</sub> and the same IR absorption region.

The equation for the hydrolysis of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> with aqueous sodium hydroxide is:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> (l) + NaOH (aq) → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> (l) + NaBr (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical formulae: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> + NaBr
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (l), (aq), (l), (aq)
> 
> C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHOHCH<sub>3</sub> may also be written as CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. The OH<sup>−</sup> ion from NaOH replaces the Br atom attached to the carbon chain.
> 
> To deduce the state symbols, use Table 1.1:
> 
> - The boiling points of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub> (364 K) and alcohol **A** (373 K) are both above room temperature (~298 K), so both are liquids (l)
> - NaOH is dissolved in water, so it is aqueous (aq)
> - NaBr is a soluble salt, so it forms an aqueous solution (aq)

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Alcohol **A** can be prepared by hydrolysing the halogenoalkane C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The melting and boiling point information of alcohol **A** and C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ are given in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **melting point / K** | **boiling point / K** |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| alcohol **A** | 158 | 373 |
| C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ | 161 | 364 |

Using the information in Table 1.1, explain how alcohol **A** can be separated from the products identified in part **(a)**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Alcohol **A** can be separated using the following steps:
> 
> - Distil the reaction mixture
> **AND**
> To remove NaBr (aq) from the organic/aqueous mixture **[1 mark]**
> - Cool the distillate to approximately 0 °C
> **AND**
> Water freezes (mp 273 K) while alcohol **A** remains liquid (mp 158 K), using the data in Table 1.1 **[1 mark]**
> - Filter the cooled mixture
> **AND**
> To remove the solid ice, leaving liquid alcohol **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> The separating funnel method is also accepted: add an organic solvent to dissolve alcohol **A**, separate the organic layer using a separating funnel, then distil off the solvent to obtain pure alcohol **A**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key challenge here is that alcohol **A** and water have the same boiling point (373 K), so simple distillation cannot separate them.
> 
> The question specifically tells you to use Table 1.1, where the key data is the melting points. The melting point of alcohol **A** is 158 K, much lower than water (273 K). Cooling to just below 0 °C freezes the water while alcohol **A** stays liquid. The solid ice can then be removed by filtration.
> 
> An alternative is the separating funnel method: dissolve alcohol **A** in an organic solvent (such as ether), which forms a separate organic layer. Use a separating funnel to drain off the aqueous layer, then distil the organic layer to remove the solvent.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Alcohol **A** can be prepared by hydrolysing the halogenoalkane C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ with aqueous sodium hydroxide.

The equation for the hydrolysis of C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ with aqueous sodium hydroxide is:

C~2~H~5~CHBrCH~3~ (l) + NaOH (aq) → C~2~H~5~CHOHCH~3~ (l) + NaBr (aq)

Describe **two** chemical tests and their expected observations to confirm the identity of the inorganic product of the reaction in part **(a)**. Use one test for each ion.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> To confirm the identity of the inorganic product:
> 
> Na<sup>+</sup> ion:
> 
> - Flame test
> **AND**
> Yellow / orange flame **[1 mark]**
> 
> Br<sup>−</sup> ion:
> 
> - Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution / acidified AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq)
> **AND**
> A cream precipitate forms **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The inorganic product is sodium bromide (NaBr). To confirm its identity, test for both ions.
> 
> Na<sup>+</sup> ion = flame test:
> 
> - Dip a clean nichrome wire in the solution and hold it in a Bunsen flame
> - A yellow/orange colour confirms Na<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Br<sup>−</sup> ion = silver nitrate test:
> 
> - Add dilute nitric acid first (to remove any carbonate or sulfite ions that would interfere), then add silver nitrate solution
> - A cream precipitate of silver bromide (AgBr) confirms Br<sup>−</sup>
> - AgBr is partially soluble in concentrated ammonia solution, distinguishing it from white AgCl (soluble in dilute ammonia) and yellow AgI (insoluble in ammonia)

parts.problem_md:
The mass spectrum of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Mass spectrum of 2-methylpropan-1-ol showing base peak at m/e = 43](assets/033-mass-spectrum-of-2-methylpropan-1-ol-showing-bas.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Deduce the formula of the fragment ion responsible for the peak with the greatest relative abundance.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formula of the fragment ion responsible for the peak with the greatest relative abundance is:
> 
> - (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The peak with the greatest relative abundance is the base peak. From Fig. 1.2, the base peak is at *m*/*e* = 43.
> 
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>OH is 74. A fragment at *m*/*e* = 43 is formed by loss of CH<sub>2</sub>OH (mass 31) from the molecular ion:
> 
> - 74 − 31 = 43 → fragment is (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>
> 
> The (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup> (isopropyl cation) is stabilised by the two electron-donating methyl groups, making it the most abundant fragment.
> 
> Always include the <sup>+</sup> charge when writing fragment ion formulae as it is required for the mark.

parts.problem_md: Explain how infrared spectroscopy can provide information about the bonds present in an organic molecule.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Infrared spectroscopy can provide information about bonds in an organic molecule because:
> 
> - IR radiation causes bonds within a molecule to vibrate / stretch / bend **[1 mark]**
> - Different bonds absorb IR radiation at characteristic wavenumber ranges, identifying the functional groups / bonds present **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For this type of question, link the mechanism (IR radiation causes bond vibrations) to the outcome (different bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumber ranges, allowing functional groups to be identified). Simply stating that IR identifies functional groups without explaining the underlying process will not score marks.

The alcohol from part (b) is fully oxidised by refluxing with acidified potassium dichromate solution.

Use Table 3.1 to explain how infrared spectroscopy could prove that the reaction has taken place.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Infrared spectroscopy could prove the reaction has taken place because:
> 
> - A broad absorption at 2500–3000 cm<sup>–1</sup> would appear, showing an O–H bond in a carboxyl group
> **AND**
> An absorption at 1670–1740 cm<sup>–1</sup> would appear, showing a C=O / carboxyl group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Full oxidation of a primary alcohol produces a carboxylic acid. To prove the reaction is complete, look for evidence of both the broad O–H absorption (2500–3000 cm<sup>–1</sup>) and the C=O carboxyl absorption (1670–1740 cm<sup>–1</sup>) in the product spectrum. The alcohol O–H absorption at 3200–3600 cm<sup>–1</sup> would no longer be present.
